prime.problem: A model can't learn from "a file of names" directly. It learns from individual predictions, so before any counting or training you have to decide what one example is. Get that wrong and the model can't start a name, can't stop one, or can only repeat names it has seen.
prime.fits: This is the first card of the bigram lecture. The toolkit gave you Python lists, zip and probability distributions; this card turns names.txt into the (given, next) pairs that every later card counts, samples from and trains on.
prime.goal: Explain why a bigram model sees 228,146 examples rather than 32,033, and produce those pairs for any word with zip.

attend: Why does zip(w, w[1:]) on 'emma' miss two of the examples the model needs, and which two behaviours would the model then never learn?
Which part of the len(w) + 1 count comes from letters, and which from the '.' padding?
What does picking characters (not whole names) as tokens buy you when you later sample new names?
Why does a single '.' serve as both the start and the end marker without confusing the model?
If a name appears twice in the file, what happens to its bigrams in the counts?

must: A model learns one prediction at a time → the unit of data is a (given, next) pair, not a name → 32,033 names become 228,146 examples, one per character to predict
No boundary token → zip(w, w[1:]) gives only len − 1 inner pairs → nothing teaches which letter starts a name or when to stop → pad with '.' at both ends to get len + 1 pairs
Tokens are characters, not whole names → any string of the 26 letters is reachable → the model can invent names instead of only repeating the 29,494 it has seen
'.' only ever appears as the given character at a start and as the next character at an end → one token can play both roles → 27 tokens instead of 28, with no always-empty row or column
elevated: Each copy of a repeated name is counted (2,539 names appear twice) → those names' bigrams weigh double in every count and in the loss
reference: the video's first version uses <S> and <E> before switching to '.' at 0:20:54

compress.prompt: From memory, explain in 3–5 sentences how names.txt becomes training data for a bigram model, and why the count is 228,146 rather than 32,033. Or draw 'emma' turning into its examples.
checklist: pad each name with '.' at both ends so starts and stops are learned too
a name of length n gives n + 1 examples; emma gives .e em mm ma a.
total = letters + one ending per name = 196,113 + 32,033 = 228,146
characters as tokens: 26 letters + '.' = 27, and new names are possible

retrieve.q: Explain why the number of training examples for this model is 228,146 and not 32,033.
answer: the model makes one prediction per example
each name contributes one prediction per letter plus one for the ending

retrieve.q: Walk through what chs = ['.'] + list(w) + ['.'] and zip(chs, chs[1:]) produce for 'ava', and say what each pair teaches the model.
answer: '.a' teaches that names often start with a; 'av' and 'va' teach inner transitions; 'a.' teaches that a name can end after a

retrieve.q: Karpathy first uses separate <S> and <E> tokens, then one '.'. What does each choice cost, and why is it safe to merge them?
answer: two tokens: 28×28 table with a row (after <E>) and a column (before <S>) that are always zero
one token: 27×27 and no wasted cells
safe because '.' as the given character always means 'start', and as the next character always means 'end'; the two roles never collide

retrieve.q: Someone proposes a model that treats each whole name as one token. What does it gain and what can it never do?
answer: gain: every output is a real name
loss: it can only pick among the 29,494 names it has seen
it can't invent a new name, which is the point of makemore

compare.q: This card pads with one '.' and pairs each character with its neighbour; the MLP card pads with '...' and uses 3 characters of context. What stays the same about the dataset, what changes, and why does the change matter?
answer: same: one example per character to predict, so still len + 1 per name and 228,146 in total
different: the input is the last 3 characters, not 1
more context lets the model use more of the name, but a counting table over 3-character contexts gets huge, which is why the MLP learns embeddings

compare.q: Here each name is a separate sequence bounded by '.'; in the GPT lecture the text is one long stream cut into chunks. What design choice causes the difference, and how could each one fail?
answer: names are short, independent items, so explicit start/end tokens make sense
Shakespeare is continuous text, so every position in a chunk is an example and there is no per-item boundary
bigrams fail by forgetting everything but the last character; chunked text can fail when a chunk starts mid-sentence with no earlier context

predict.q: You switch to a trigram model: each example uses the previous two characters, and each name is padded with two dots at the start and one at the end. How many examples does names.txt give now?
predict.answer: Still 228,146. There is still exactly one example per character to predict (every letter plus the final '.'); only the amount of context on the input side changes.

apply.task: Edit the lab (or your own script) to deduplicate the names with set(words) before counting. Print the number of distinct names, the total letters, and the total bigrams, and check the total equals letters + names.
apply.done: You get 29,494 distinct names, 181,834 letters and 211,328 bigrams (181,834 + 29,494), compared with 228,146 for the full file.
apply.hint: u = set(words), then sum(len(w) + 1 for w in u). Think about whether Karpathy would want repeats removed.
